sections.content:
ACTION7 did nothing (board_changed: False, no diff). Might be a no-op, or might need a selection. Not useful.
Let me think more carefully. Reconsider the problem. Maybe the win condition isn't about the top row at all. Let me look at the level 1 board again and check what was special. Level 1: top row [b,N,Y,p], box with 4 slots, palette at the bottom with 4 tiles. Filled the box with [b,N,Y,p] and SPACE → cleared.
Wait — in level 1, did the palette tiles get consumed? The palette at the bottom of the level 1 start (row 58) had tiles. I moved them into the box. The top row showed the target order.
Level 2: no bottom palette; the top row has 7 squares. But wait — maybe in level 2 the top row is the palette (draggable source), and the target is shown elsewhere! In level 1, the top row was the target, and the palette was at the bottom. In level 2, the "palette" is the top row (7 squares), and the target is… the anchor + green line? The target might be implicit: the red box should contain… hmm.
Or in level 2, the top row is the palette, and the target is: the red box = the first 4 of the top row? The green box = the last 4? With 7 squares and 8 slots, there's overlap: red = [O,p,R,b]?? But the anchor N is at red slot 3, which conflicts with R.
Unless the anchor isn't fixed! What if the anchor can be moved? The anchor is a c (charcoal) square with an N border… actually the anchor is rendered as a small square with a green border and a c interior — a distinctive marker. If movable, the target might be red=[O,p,R,b], green=[N,Y,M,?].
Hmm, let me look at the anchor's appearance: at (22,34) it's 'c' with a border. In the image, it's a small green-outlined square. Maybe it's a "cursor" or "marker" indicating the current position within the sequence! Like a playhead: the sequence is the top row (7 elements), and the marker is at position 3 of the red box. The goal might be to arrange the tiles so the marker ends up at the correct position…
New idea: maybe the puzzle is "reconstruct the sequence": the 8 slots form a sequence; the top row shows the target sequence with the marker element removed; the marker (N) must be placed at the position where it belongs in the target. Where does N belong in the top row [O,p,R,b,N,Y,M]? N is at position 5 of the top row. But the marker is at position 3 of the red box. If the top row is the complete target (7 elements) and the marker indicates the 8th position… no, that's not right.
Wait, actually: the top row is the target sequence of 7, the 8 slots = 7 target positions + 1 extra, and the marker occupies the extra position (position 3)? Then the target: position 3 = marker N, the other positions = the top row in order skipping… no: 7 top row elements fill 7 non-marker slots in order: [O,p,_,R,b,N,Y,M] → position 3 is the marker, so the top row maps to positions 1,2,4,5,6,7,8: pos1=O, pos2=p, pos4=R, pos5=b, pos6=N, pos7=Y, pos8=M. Sequence = [O,p,N,R,b,N,Y,M]. Red=[O,p,N,R], green=[b,N,Y,M] — hypothesis 3, already tried ✗.
Or the top row maps to positions 1,2,3,4,5,6,7 (the marker is at position 8)? But the marker is at position 3. ✗.
Hmm, what if the marker's position within the box (slot 3 of 8) means N is the 3rd element, and the top row is the remaining 7 in order: [O,p,N,R,b,N,Y,M] — same as above ✗.
So the "sequence" family is exhausted (both red=[O,p,N,R] and red=[R,b,N,Y] variants tried… wait, the sequence family gives red=[O,p,N,R], green=[b,N,Y,M] ✗).
The "overlap" family gives red=[R,b,N,Y], green={O,p,M,N} in some order; tried [O,p,M,N] ✗, [O,p,N,M] ✗.
Let me enumerate the overlap family more cleverly. The green box is below the red box. Maybe the green box order = the top row order of the remaining squares, but the top row order of the remaining is [O,p,M], and N goes where the line points (g3): [O,p,N,M] ✗. Or N at the front: [N,O,p,M]? Or the line points to the green box in general (not a specific slot).
Honestly, maybe I should reconsider: the green box target = [O,p,M,N] but the red box isn't [R,b,N,Y]! What if the red box = [R,b,N,Y] is wrong because the N square (36-41) overlaps slot 3 (33-38) and slot 4 (39-42)?? 36-41 overlaps 33-38 (36,37,38) and 39-42 (39,40,41) — both! And the Y (43-48) overlaps slot 4 (39-42)? No: 43-48 vs 39-42: no overlap (43>42). Hmm wait, slot 4 is columns 39-42. Y is 43-48. No overlap. So Y doesn't overlap any slot! Then the red box target from overlap is: R→s1, b→s2, N→s3/s4 (ambiguous), and Y→none. So red = [R,b,N,?] with ? unknown, and Y goes to the green box!
Then the green box = {Y, O, p, M} + … 4 slots: O, p, M, Y — exactly 4! And N is only the anchor (not duplicated)! But wait, the movable tiles include N (the 7th square). If N is only the anchor… the N square in the top row must also be placed somewhere. Hmm, no: the 7 squares = 7 movable tiles. The N square is movable. So the final board has 2 Ns (anchor + tile).
Unless the N square in the top row is a marker for the anchor (not a tile)! Then the movable tiles = 6: O,p,R,b,Y,M, filling 6 slots… but there are 7 empty slots. ✗. Unless one slot stays empty! Maybe the goal is to fill only 7 of the 8 slots, leaving one empty!
Oh, this is a new idea: the final board has 7 tiles (the 7 squares of the top row) + the anchor, with one slot empty. Which slot? Maybe the green line indicates an empty slot in the green box! The line points to g3 → g3 is empty!
Then: red = [R,b,N,Y] (overlap: R→s1, b→s2, N→s3, Y→s4 — wait, Y doesn't overlap s4… hmm).
Let me redo the overlap with the actual columns. Top squares: O(8-13), p(15-20), R(22-27), b(29-34), N(36-41), Y(43-48), M(50-55). Red box slots: s1(21-24), s2(27-30), s3(33-38, anchor), s4(39-42).
- R(22-27) ∩ s1(21-24) = {22,23,24} ✓; ∩ s2(27-30) = {27} (1 column).
- b(29-34) ∩ s2(27-30) = {29,30} ✓; ∩ s3(33-38) = {33,34}.
- N(36-41) ∩ s3(33-38) = {36,37,38} ✓; ∩ s4(39-42) = {39,40,41}.
- Y(43-48) ∩ s4(39-42) = {} ✗.
So Y and M don't overlap the red slots. The red box from overlap: R→s1, b→s2, N→s3 (anchor ✓ consistent!), s4 = ? (from the remaining O,p,Y,M).
Hmm, so s4 could be O, p, Y, or M. And the green box gets the other 3 + …
This is getting complicated. The anchor N at s3 is consistent with the N square overlapping s3 — good, the anchor is a hint that N belongs at s3.
So red = [R, b, N, X], X ∈ {O,p,Y,M}; green = the remaining 3 + the 4th.
Total 7 tiles: {O,p,R,b,N,Y,M}: red uses R,b,N,X; green uses the remaining 4 = {O,p,Y,M} \ {X} + … wait, 7 - 4 = 3, but the green box has 4 slots. So one green slot is empty!
So: red = [R,b,N,X], green = 3 tiles + 1 empty.
Where's the empty? Maybe where the green line points (g3)? Or the empty is indicated by the line's target…
Candidates: X ∈ {O,p,Y,M} (4 options) × empty position (4) × green order (3! = 6) = 96. Too many to brute force blindly.
But wait — is this consistent with level 1? Level 1: 4 squares, 4 slots, no anchor, no empty. Filled everything. No problem.
Hmm, but actually, why would there be an empty slot? The green line might indicate "this slot is empty" — a "skip" marker!
Or the line indicates that the anchor's color (N) goes into that green slot, and there's no empty (the 8th tile = a duplicate N). That was the earlier hypothesis: green = {O,p,M,N} (X=Y: red=[R,b,N,Y]). Tried 2 orders ✗.
Or X=O: red=[R,b,N,O], green={p,Y,M,N}: order?
I need more signal. Let me look at the anchor's green line more carefully: from the anchor (rows 22-27, columns 33-38) down to the top edge of the green box (row 33). Column ~35. Green box slots: g1(21-24), g2(27-30), g3(33-36), g4(39-42). Column 35 → g3.
If the line means "N goes into g3": candidates with N at g3:
- X=Y: green={O,p,M,N} with N at g3: [O,p,N,M] ✗ tried.
- X=O: green={p,Y,M,N} with N at g3: [p,Y,N,M], [Y,p,N,M].
- X=p: green={O,Y,M,N} with N at g3: [O,Y,N,M], [Y,O,N,M].
- X=M: green={O,p,Y,N} with N at g3: [O,p,N,Y], [p,O,N,Y].
If the line means "g3 is empty":
- X=Y: green={O,p,M} with g3 empty: [O,p,_,M], [M,p,_,O], [O,_,p,M], etc.
Too many.
Let me think about the design intent again. Actually, you know what? Let me reconsider the whole thing. Maybe the two boxes are two separate sub-puzzles, each with its own target shown by the squares above it:
- The red box's target = the squares above it: R, b, N, Y (in column order) → red=[R,b,N,Y].
- The green box's target = the squares above it… the red box is above it. The red box's contents after solving = [R,b,N,Y]. So the green box's target = [R,b,N,Y]?? But those tiles are in the red box. Unless the green box's target is the red box's target shifted by the line: the line from the anchor (s3) to the green box means "the green box starts from the anchor's position": green = [N, Y, O, p]? (wrap around the top row: from N: N,Y,M,O? or N,Y,M,p?)
Top row from N (position 5) wrapping: N, Y, M, O → green=[N,Y,M,O]? New candidate!
Or green = the top row from position 5: [N,Y,M] + the first = O: [N,Y,M,O].
Or the green box = the top row from position 5 to the end + wrap: N,Y,M,O,p — take 4: [N,Y,M,O].
Let me try green=[N,Y,M,O] with red=[R,b,N,Y].
Current: red=[O,p,N,R], green=[b,Y,M,N].
To red=[R,b,N,Y]: swap r1/r4 (O↔R), swap r2/r3? No: r=[O,p,N,R] → [R,b,N,Y]: r1: O→R, r2: p→b, r4: R→Y. Move: R to r1, b to r2, Y to r4.
To green=[N,Y,M,O]: g=[b,Y,M,N] → g1: b→N, g4: N→O. Swap g1/g4 → g=[N,Y,M,b]; then b→O: b is in g1… wait, after the swap g1=N, g4=b. Need g4=O, and O is in r1 (after the red fix, r1=R… O is in r4? No: after the red fix, red=[R,b,N,Y], O is in green. Hmm, O is currently in r1.
This is getting complicated. Let me plan the moves:
Current: r=[O,p,N,R] (r1=O, r2=p, r4=R), g=[b,Y,M,N] (g1=b, g2=Y, g3=M, g4=N).
Target: r=[R,b,N,Y], g=[N,Y,M,O].
Final positions: R: r1, b: r2, Y: r4, N (tile): g1, O: g4, M: g3, p: ??? — wait, p has to go somewhere! 7 tiles: O,p,R,b,N,Y,M. Target red uses R,b,N (anchor),Y → movable in red: R,b,Y. Green: N,O + … g=[N,Y,M,O] uses Y twice! ✗. Y can't be in both.
Right — the tiles are unique. Red=[R,b,N,Y] uses Y; green can't have Y. So green=[N,Y,M,O] is invalid.
OK, so with red=[R,b,N,Y], green ⊆ {O,p,M,N}.
With the line→g3=N: [O,p,N,M] ✗ tried.
So the next best: try [N,O,p,M], [N,p,O,M], [M,N,O,p], [M,N,p,O], [p,N,O,M], [p,N,M,O], [O,N,p,M], [O,N,M,p], [M,O,N,p], [M,p,N,O], [p,O,N,M], [p,M,N,O], [O,M,N,p], [O,M,p,N], [M,O,p,N], [M,p,O,N], [p,O,M,N], [p,M,O,N], [N,M,O,p], [N,M,p,O], [N,O,M,p], [N,p,M,O].
22 candidates. Timer ~39. Each trial: up to 2 swaps + SPACE ≈ 3-4 steps → ~10 trials. Not enough.
Need a smarter discriminator. Idea: test whether the red box alone matters: set red=[R,b,N,Y] and green to any permutation, submit → if it fails, try a different red. But each submission only gives binary info.
Better idea: find a submission that's correct under multiple hypotheses at once (a "covering" candidate). Or use the structure: maybe the order within the green box follows the same rule as level 1: each tile goes below its top square, but for the green box, "below" wraps around: the green box is below the red box, and the red box is below the top row. The squares O(8-13), p(15-20) are to the left of the red box; M(50-55) is to the right. Maybe they "fall" into the green box by wrapping around the edges: O and p fall down the left side → g1, g2 (in order O, p); M falls down the right side → g4; N (the anchor's color, via the line) → g3. Green = [O,p,N,M] ✗ tried!! Argh.
Or M→g4, O→g1, p→g2, N→g3: same [O,p,N,M] ✗.
Or the left-side squares go in reverse: p→g1, O→g2: [p,O,N,M]? New.
Or M→g1 (wrapping to the front)? [M,O,p,N]?
Hmm, let me try [p,O,N,M] — no wait, let me think about which is more likely.
Actually, let me step back and reconsider whether red=[R,b,N,Y] is even correct. Hypothesis 1 was red=[R,b,N,Y], green=[O,p,M,N] — failed. If the win condition is set-based per box (order-independent), hypothesis 1 should have passed (red set {R,b,N,Y} ✓, green set {O,p,M,N} ✓). It failed → the win condition is order-dependent (or the sets are wrong).
Given the strong overlap evidence for red=[R,b,N,Y], the green order must be one of the remaining 22.
Let me think about the green line once more. It's green (N color). It connects the anchor to the green box. In the image, it looks like a vertical line from the bottom of the anchor to the top edge of the green box, at column ~35 (g3).
Maybe the line means: the green box's sequence starts from the anchor: i.e., read the top row starting from N: N, Y, M, then wrap O, p → the green box = [N,Y,M,O]… but Y is used in red. ✗ (if red=[R,b,N,Y]).
Unless red isn't [R,b,N,Y]! What if the Y square (43-48) doesn't belong to the red box because it doesn't overlap s4? Then red = [R,b,N,X] with X ∈ {O,p,M}, and Y goes to the green box!
Then green = {Y, O, p, M} \ {X} + … 4 slots: if X=O: green={p,Y,M}+? — only 3. ✗. Wait, 7 tiles: red uses R,b,N,X (4 including anchor? No — the anchor isn't a tile). Red's movable = R,b,X (3 tiles). Green's movable = 4 tiles = {O,p,Y,M}\{X} + … that's 3. Total movable = 6 ≠ 7. ✗. So one slot is empty, or N is duplicated.
I keep going in circles. Time to get empirical: run a structured search with the timer in mind. Actually, wait — let me check the timer more carefully. Does the timer really decrease per action, or per submission? Frame 58: bar 0-39 (40 units). Let me check the bar length at the start of level 2 (frame 24) and a few in between to get the rate. If it decreases per MOUSE/SPACE action, I have ~39 units ≈ 10-13 trials. If only per SPACE, more.
Also: what happens at 0? Probably game over. Risky.
Alternative: maybe there's a way to get more feedback from a wrong submission — e.g., the board flashes or a wrong slot gets marked. My diff check after SPACE showed no change… but the flash might be transient (only in the returned frame, then reverts). The returned frame after a wrong SPACE showed the same board. So no feedback.
OK, let me prioritize the candidates by design plausibility:
1. [O,p,N,M] ✗
2. [O,p,M,N] ✗
3. [p,O,N,M] (left-side squares in reverse)
4. [N,O,p,M] (N first, line points to the front?)
5. [M,N,O,p] (right-side square first?)
6. [N,M,O,p]
7. [M,O,p,N]
8. [O,M,p,N]
Hmm. Actually, wait. Let me reconsider the geometry: the green line is at column ~35. Let me get the exact column from the segmentation (the N node at rows 28-32). If the line is at column 35 → g3 (33-36). If 34-35 → g3.
And the anchor is at s3 (33-38). The line is directly below the anchor.
New thought: maybe the line + anchor means: the anchor's position (s3) is a "pivot": the top row is split at N (position 5): left part [O,p,R,b] (4 squares), right part [Y,M] (2 squares). The red box = the left part in reverse? [b,R,p,O]… the anchor is at s3 ✗.
Or the red box = [R,b] + anchor + [Y,M]?? Red = [R,b,N,Y] with M→s4? No, M is at 50-55.
Red = [R,b,N,Y]: R (position 3), b (position 4) are before N (position 5), Y (position 6) is after. So red = the 2 before + N + the 1 after! And the green box = the remaining: O (position 1), p (position 2), M (position 7) + … 4 slots, 3 squares. The 4th = N again (the line) or empty.
If the 4th = N: the order might be: [O,p,M,N] ✗ or by distance from N: O (distance 4), p (distance 3), M (distance 2) → [M,p,O,N]? Or [O,p,M,N] ✗.
If the 4th = empty: the order [O,p,M,_] or [_,O,p,M]…
Let me try [M,p,O,N] — no, let me think about the most natural for a game designer: the green box is a "continuation" of the sequence after the red box. Red = [R,b,N,Y] (positions 3,4,5,6). The sequence continues: position 7 = M, then wraps to positions 1,2 = O,p. Green = [M,O,p,?] with ? = N (the line) or empty. [M,O,p,N]! New candidate.
Or the green box = the part before the red box: positions 1,2 = O,p, then… [O,p,?,?] with ? = M (position 7, wrapping) and N: [O,p,M,N] ✗ tried.
So [M,O,p,N] is the "continuation" candidate. Let me try it.
Current: r=[O,p,N,R], g=[b,Y,M,N]. Target: r=[R,b,N,Y], g=[M,O,p,N].
Moves:
- r1=O → g2 (target g2=O). r4=R → r1. r2=p → g3. g1=b → r2. g2=Y → r4. g3=M → g1. g4=N stays.
Cycle: O: r1→g2; Y: g2→r4; R: r4→r1; b: g1→r2; p: r2→g3; M: g3→g1. Two 3-cycles: (r1→g2→r4→r1): O→g2, Y→r4, R→r1. And (g1→r2→g3→g1): b→r2, p→g3, M→g1.
Execution (swap-based):
Cycle A: r1=O, g2=Y, r4=R → target r1=R, g2=O, r4=Y.
- Select r1 (O), click r4 (R) → r1=R, r4=O.
- Select r4 (O), click g2 (Y) → r4=Y, g2=O. ✓ Cycle A done: r1=R, r4=Y, g2=O.
Cycle B: g1=b, r2=p, g3=M → target g1=M, r2=b, g3=p.
- Select g1 (b), click r2 (p) → g1=p, r2=b.
- Select g1 (p), click g3 (M) → g1=M, g3=p. ✓ Cycle B done.
Result: r=[R,b,N,Y], g=[M,O,p,N].
Then SPACE.
Total 6 mouse + 1 space = 7 steps. Timer 39 → 32. OK.
If it fails, remaining candidates: [M,O,p,_ empty], [M,p,O,N], [p,O,N,M], [N,O,p,M], [N,M,O,p], [O,M,p,N], [p,M,O,N], [M,N,O,p], [M,N,p,O], [p,N,O,M], [p,N,M,O], [O,N,p,M], [O,N,M,p], [N,O,M,p], [N,M,p,O], [N,p,O,M], [N,p,M,O], [M,p,N,O], [M,O,N,p], [p,O,M,N], [p,M,N,O]…
Let me execute [M,O,p,N] now.

Green = {O,p,M,N}; the "continuation" rule (sequence continues past the red box: M, then wraps to O, p, N via the line) gives green=[M,O,p,N] — untried.
Plan: Rearrange to red=[R,b,N,Y], green=[M,O,p,N] (two 3-cycles), then SPACE.
